extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in comedy/humor
extracted.subtask_description: Understand, evaluate, or produce off-color (vulgar/crude/shock) humor by identifying defining topics, purposes, genres, delivery techniques, cultural framing, historical context, and legal/social risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: humor dealing with vulgar or poor-taste topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Off-color humor (also known as vulgar humor, crude humor, crass humor, coarse humor or shock humor) is humor that deals with topics that may be considered to be in poor taste or vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core definitional standard: material qualifies as off-color if it centers on subjects commonly judged indecent or vulgar. The page notes synonyms and that many comedic genres may incorporate such elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects that commonly make material 'off-color'
rubrics_metrics.description: Most commonly labeled as 'off-color' are acts concerned with sex, a particular ethnic group, or gender. Other off-color topics include violence (particularly domestic abuse); excessive swearing or profanity; toilet humor; national superiority or inferiority; pedophilic content; and any topics generally considered impolite or indecent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or crafting off-color humor, check whether the subject matter falls into these categories — they are explicit markers of 'off-color' status. The list signals both common targets and higher-risk taboos (e.g., pedophilia, domestic abuse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose/effect: to induce laughter via shock and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the point of off-color humor is to induce laughter by evoking a feeling of shock and surprise in the comedian's audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate success by the extent to which the material provokes shocked surprise that produces laughter. The page ties this purpose to related forms like postmodern humor and the anti-joke, indicating that surprise and boundary-violation are central mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre/format inclusion: which comedic forms may incorporate off-color elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Many comedic genres (including jokes, prose, poems, black comedy, blue comedy, insult comedy, cringe comedy and skits) may incorporate 'off-color' elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should note that off-color content can appear across formats — stand-up, sketches, cartoons, prose — and that format may shape tone, acceptable extremity, and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social function: subversion and social commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Off-color humor has been used as an effective tool for social commentary and subversion, drawing attention to issues such as censorship and socioeconomic divides; historically some dirty jokes were considered subversive and underground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the creator's intent: is the offense deployed for critique or social commentary? The page cites practitioners (e.g., George Carlin, Richard Pryor, Bill Hicks, Dave Chappelle) who used shocking content to highlight social issues — this contextualizes offensiveness as a rhetorical device rather than gratuitous insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery techniques: shock, outrageous stunts, absurdity, and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have used shocking content and outrageous stunts (e.g., Tom Green), absurdist approaches (e.g., Dave Attell, Louis C.K.), and sustained raunchy stand-up to produce off-color effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating off-color humor, examine the chosen delivery methods — physical stunts, absurdism, explicit language, or persona — and whether they align with audience expectations and the intended effect (shock, satire, absurdity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural framing and terminology (e.g., 'veg' vs 'non-veg')
rubrics_metrics.description: In some parts of the world, sexual humor is known as 'non-veg' humor, contrasted with the 'veg' jokes that are more acceptable in polite company. The term reflects cultural dietary metaphors and differing norms about what is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work with sensitivity to local cultural framings and labels; what is acceptable or labeled 'off-color' varies by region and cultural context. Use of local terms signals differing boundaries and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience acceptance and historical change in tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: American society has become increasingly tolerant of off-color humor since the 1960s; mainstream success of certain comedians and shows has shifted what is socially acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess acceptability relative to temporal and cultural context — material once subversive may now be mainstream. Consider historical norms when judging offensiveness and likely audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/obscenity risk and potential consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Dirty jokes were once considered subversive and underground; Lenny Bruce was tried, convicted, and jailed for obscenity after a stand-up performance that included off-color humor in 1964.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or distributing off-color material, factor in legal and community standards (obscenity laws, broadcast regulations). Historical examples show real legal risk and consequences may apply depending on jurisdiction and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical use in media and platforms (television, animation, clubs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Off-color humor has been presented in nightclubs, television (often toned down), cartoons (Beavis and Butt-head, South Park), film, and books; medium affects permissible explicitness and audience reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate suitability of content against the chosen medium: clubs permit more raunch; network TV often requires toning down; animation can push boundaries differently. Medium shapes style, censorship, and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical boundary marker: targeting vs. commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Off-color topics often target sex, ethnic groups, gender, etc.; creators vary between attacking targets (insult/punching-down) and using taboo topics for commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether material punches down (targets vulnerable groups gratuitously) or uses taboo subject matter to critique power or social norms. This distinction matters for ethical evaluation and audience reception.
